title: Type hierarchy on a page — Image Wiki
text:
Type hierarchy on a page
  How a reader finds their way through a page without being told — by size, weight, space, position and case. Space does more of the work than size does.

  
    Termtypographic hierarchy
    Also calledtype hierarchy, heading levels, information hierarchy
    Not the same asvisual hierarchy, font pairing, readability
    Read8 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        Space does more than sizeVignelli's two sizesThe other three leversCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Look at a page of a magazine you have never opened and notice that you did not have to decide where to start. You went to the title, then the standfirst, then either into the body or out again. No arrows, no numbers, nobody told you the order.
That order is typographic hierarchy, made from five levers: size, weight, space, position and case. People reach for size first, and it is the weakest of them.
Space does more than size

SUMMER SHOWSRiverside ParkConcerts every Saturday at 6.Free entry, no ticket needed.Bring a blanket, not glass.Buses 12 and 40 stop outside.Only cancelled in heavy rain.GETTING THEREEnter by the north gate.Bike racks by the cafe.Riverside Parks TrustNo hierarchyone size, even leadingSUMMER SHOWSRiverside ParkConcerts every Saturday at 6.Free entry, no ticket needed.Bring a blanket, not glass.Buses 12 and 40 stop outside.Only cancelled in heavy rain.GETTING THEREEnter by the north gate.Bike racks by the cafe.Riverside Parks TrustSpace onlyone size, gaps between groupsSUMMER SHOWSRiverside ParkConcerts every Saturday at 6.Free entry, no ticket needed.Bring a blanket, not glass.Buses 12 and 40 stop outside.Only cancelled in heavy rain.GETTING THEREEnter by the north gate.Bike racks by the cafe.Riverside Parks TrustSize onlyfive sizes, no gaps

The same eleven lines of a park notice, three times. Left, one size, one leading, no gaps: a wall. You can read it, but you cannot see it — finding the address means reading every line until you hit it.
Middle, still one size everywhere. The only change is empty lines between the groups, and now the page has four visible parts. Right, no gaps at all, but five type sizes doing the separating. It works too, and notice what it feels like: busier, more insistent, and the small last line has been pushed toward the illegible.
Middle and right cost the same effort and solve the same problem. The middle one is calmer and did not touch a single type size. That is the ranking in a nutshell — grouping by proximity, which is one of the Gestalt grouping rules, is a stronger and cheaper signal than magnitude.


Space works by grouping; size works by ranking. Grouping tells you what belongs with what, which is the question you actually have on an unfamiliar page. Ranking only tells you which item is loudest — and four things shouting at four volumes still has not said which three of them are one thought.
A reliable failure follows. If your headings feel weak the reflex is to enlarge them, and it rarely helps, because the heading is not losing a size contest with the body text — it is failing to look separate from it. The fix is space above it. Vignelli's own default is exactly that: keep heads and subheads at the body size, set them bold, and put a line space above and none below, so the heading visibly belongs to the paragraph it introduces (The Vignelli Canon, p. 35).
Vignelli's two sizes

SUMMER SHOWSTwelve weekends of musicPROGRAMMESaturdays and Sundays from 6 pm.Free entry to all main stages.Bar and food until midnight.No glass bottles on site.GETTING THERENorth gate, off Mill Lane.Buses 12 and 40 stop outside.Riverside Parks Trust, since 1904.Five sizes on one page26 / 17 / 14 / 11 / 9.5 ptSUMMER SHOWSTwelve weekends of musicPROGRAMMESaturdays and Sundays from 6 pm.Free entry to all main stages.Bar and food until midnight.No glass bottles on site.GETTING THERENorth gate, off Mill Lane.Buses 12 and 40 stop outside.Riverside Parks Trust, since 1904.Two sizes on one page22 and 11 pt; bold and space do the rest

The same content, five sizes against two. Right uses 22 pt and 11 pt — Vignelli's preferred doubling — and gets its four levels from weight (bold section heads at body size), from space, and from lightening the last line rather than shrinking it.
Look at what the left panel spent to reach the same clarity: two extra sizes, one of them small enough to be a problem, and a page whose rhythm changes on nearly every line. Then judge for yourself which you would rather read at a glance. It is a genuine argument, not a proof.


Two type sizes is a rule Vignelli states twice, and it is worth taking as a position rather than a law. "Basically we stick to no more then two type sizes on a printed page, but there are exceptions," he writes (p. 35), and the pairing he likes is one twice the other: 10 pt text with 20 pt headings. Where more distinction is needed, he says use bold, light, roman and italic — "but even there, stick to the minimum" (p. 37).
His reasoning is not aesthetic tidiness. The Canon puts Semantics, Syntactics, Pragmatics and Discipline (pp. 6–9) ahead of every tangible rule, and this one sits downstream of them. Size and weight, in his account, should be dedicated to a function, never used as colour or as a phonetic analogy — he does not think that writing "dog" entitles the type to bark (p. 28). Enlarging type to make a message louder he calls intellectual vulgarity, and the alternative he offers is the sentence the whole Canon turns on: "In a world where everybody screams, silence is noticeable. White space provides the silence" (p. 37).
What the rule buys. A decision you never make cannot be made inconsistently — which matters most when other people apply your layout to material you will never see. Two sizes also means two well-chosen sizes: the small one tuned to the column width (Vignelli gives 8/9, 9/10 or 10/11 pt for measures up to 70 mm, 12/13 or 14/16 up to 140 mm, 16/18 or 18/20 beyond that, p. 35) and the large one at a clean multiple, so headings can share the baseline ladder from Grids.
What it costs. Real editorial material has more than two levels. A recipe has a title, a yield, a time, an ingredient list, numbered steps and a footnote about substitutions — six, and no amount of bold separates all of them. Magazine practice goes the other way, treating type as image and lettering as message: a spread may carry six sizes and hand-drawn lettering because it is meant to be looked at as much as read (LAY-011). Vignelli's rule is a rule for organising information. It is a bad rule for a page whose job is to be a picture made of words.



Playbill of the Theatre Royal, Drury Lane, Thursday 30 September 1784, announcing The Clandestine Marriage. Bodleian Libraries, John Johnson Collection of Printed Ephemera; public domain.
The opposite position, taken to its limit: this sheet has roughly a dozen sizes and almost no space. Every line is centred on one axis, every line is a different size, and hierarchy is done by magnitude alone. The two biggest lines are the two plays; the actors' surnames are pushed up in wide-spaced capitals while their roles stay small and lower case, so Lord Ogleby by Mr. is quiet and KING is loud, in the middle of the same line.
It is not incompetence — it works, and it worked for two centuries. But count the costs. There is no first read: nothing here survives being seen from three metres away. Nothing can be skimmed, because there are no groups, only a gradient. And every new line was a fresh decision for the compositor, which is exactly what a system is meant to eliminate.





Have a Date with Us, made by NYC WPA War Services for the American Museum of Natural History, 1941. Public domain (Library of Congress).
Count the type sizes and you get about eight, which by Vignelli's standard is a mess. It is not a mess, and the reason is that almost none of the levels are marked by size alone.
Colour does the top split: everything orange is the invitation, everything olive-brown is the detail, so "FREE TO YOU / AND YOUR FRIENDS" separates from the list below it before you have read a word. Position does the next one — the whole text block sits inside a ragged white patch painted over the picture, which is what keeps eight sizes of type from fighting the totem pole. Case does the finest one: in "AMERICAN MUSEUM of NATURAL HISTORY", every word is the same size, and the emphasis comes from alternating white against brown and dropping the connective to lower case. Two words are promoted and one demoted without touching a size.
The one thing size is used for here is the diagonal red line, which is the only element aimed at someone walking past. Everything else is second-read material, sorted by other means.


The other three levers

Weight. Bold at the same size reads as emphasis within a level; it separates without changing the page's rhythm. Its weakness: it does not scale, and bold on bold on bold is nothing.
Position. A line hanging in the left margin is at a different level from one indented into the text, at identical size and weight. Position is nearly free and under-used.
Case and colour. All caps and a muted grey both mark a level. Caps cost reading speed beyond three words and grey costs contrast, so keep both for short labels.

One optical repair belongs here: hang quotation marks, bullets and hyphens slightly outside the text edge, so the column's left side looks straight rather than merely being straight (LAY-008).
Common mistakes

"Bigger means more important." Only inside one group. Across groups, size without space gives a loud page with no structure — the right-hand panel above.
"More levels means clearer." Five levels a reader cannot tell apart is one level. Merge until every level you keep is unmistakable.
Equal space above and below a heading. The commonest hierarchy bug there is: it orphans the heading between two paragraphs, so it belongs to neither.
"Two sizes is a law." It is Vignelli's discipline, argued from his practice, and he lists exceptions himself. Treat it as a default that makes you try space and weight before reaching for a third size.


Testing a page's hierarchy

Blur or shrink the page until you cannot read words. How many distinct groups can you count?
Is that the number of groups the content actually has?
Count the type sizes. For each one, name the job it does. Any size without a job goes.
Look at the space around every heading. Is there more above than below?
Cover the largest element. Can you still find your way in? If not, one element is carrying the whole structure.



  
    
      Read next
      
        
          
            
              Grids
              A set of decisions taken once — margins, columns, gutters, modules, baselines — so that no later page needs a fresh decision. It is a system, not a look.
            
          
        
          
            
              Visual hierarchy
              The order in which your eye visits the parts of an image — decided by the image, not by you.
            
          
        
          
            
              Negative space
              The empty parts of an image are shapes too, and you are composing them whether you notice or not.
            
          
        
          
            
              The first read
              What is left of a poster when you are far away and not paying attention — and the five or six tests that tell you whether that residue still carries the message.
